overview.summary: Optometrists examine eyes, test vision, detect eye conditions and prescribe glasses and contact lenses. Their legal role differs by country.
overview.problems: They help people see clearly and comfortably, and spot eye and general health problems early.
overview.worksWith: Patients of all ages, opticians and dispensers, eye doctors, family doctors and other health professionals.
overview.workplaces: Opticians' practices, eye clinics, hospitals and optical retail chains, and some run their own practice.

timeline.title: Prepare for appointments
timeline.description: The optometrist reviews records and checks equipment.

timeline.title: Eye examinations
timeline.description: The optometrist asks about symptoms and history, tests vision, checks eye health and measures the eye.
timeline.why: Early detection of problems protects sight.

timeline.title: Interpreting results
timeline.description: The optometrist works out the prescription and decides whether the patient needs further tests.
timeline.why: Correct decisions depend on careful interpretation.

timeline.title: Fitting and advice
timeline.description: The optometrist helps patients choose glasses or fits contact lenses and explains how to look after them.
timeline.why: Good fit and care make lenses comfortable and safe.

timeline.title: Records and referrals
timeline.description: The optometrist writes notes and refers patients to eye doctors or family doctors when needed.
timeline.why: Some eye problems need specialist treatment.

timeline.title: Children and older patients
timeline.description: Some patients need extra time and different approaches.
timeline.why: Eye care has to suit every age.

responsibilities: Testing vision and examining eye health
Detecting eye disease and referring when needed
challenges: Examinations are repetitive and involve long periods sitting close to patients.
Detecting serious problems and delivering difficult news is part of the job.
Some patients are nervous, including children.
There is pressure to sell products in some retail practices.
Rules about what optometrists may do differ by country.
workEnvironment: Quiet, well-lit examination rooms in clinics and practices, with regular hours and appointments. The work is one-to-one, seated and precise. Some optometrists work in hospitals or manage a business.
rewards: The option to run your own practice
tradeoffs: Pay and conditions that vary by country and setting

activity.title: Learn how the eye works and explain it
steps: Read about how the eye focuses light on a trusted source such as a national eye health or optometry association.
Draw a simple diagram of the cornea, lens, retina and optic nerve.
Learn two habits that protect eyes, such as screen breaks.
Explain them to a family member and answer one question.
Note whether the topic felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise learning anatomy and giving clear health information.
activity.safety: This is an information exercise only. Do not test anyone's eyes, shine bright lights into eyes or advise anyone on eye problems. See a qualified optometrist for real concerns.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
